newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: No APEC pact on Infotech; U.S. says still pleased.
newsitem.headline: No APEC pact on Infotech; U.S. says still pleased.

text.p: Ministers from the 18 APEC economies failed on Saturday to agree how to free trade in computers and telecommunications but the United States, main proponent of a pact to cover high technology, said it was still "delighted".

Ministers of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum emerged from two days of talks in Manila with a vaguely-worded statement on the issue, passing responsibility on to the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

"Ministers endorsed the efforts at WTO to conclude an information technology agreement by the Singapore Ministerial conference and urged all other members of the WTO to work toward that end," a joint statement read.
The WTO will hold its first ministerial conference in Singapore in December.
Washington had been pushing APEC to endorse its Information Technology Agreement (ITA), a plan to cut tariffs to zero by the year 2000 on a broad range of information technology products.
Evene though there was no accord, U.S. Commerce Secretary Mickey Kantor had only words of praise and hope for the APEC statement on Saturday.
"We think the language of endorsement is not only adequate but helpful as well as supportive," Kantor told a joint news conference after the meetings ended.
"We are delighted with the result," he said.
The stakes are high. Washington says the information technology business is worth $1.8 trillion.
The United States, which accounts for 60 percent of the business, had hoped APEC would endorse the ITA to give the pact a head start when it is submitted to the WTO in Singapore.
Malaysia and some other developing countries object to the tariff targets and timeframes in the pact, saying it undermines the essential volunteer nature of the diverse economies in APEC.
Malaysian Trade Minister Rafidah Aziz emphasised at the news conference that APEC ministers went no further than endorsing work toward an eventual agreement.
"There's no agreement here," she said definitively.
